newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr in retreat as rate futures advance.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr in retreat as rate futures advance.

text.p: The Australian dollar bowed beneath heavy offshore selling at the midsession to lie a full cent down on this time Monday.
Traders said U.S. names had been on both sides of the market but sellers had the weight advantage with up to A$500 million rumoured to have been dumped this morning.
Local exporters helped provide some support at US$0.7750 but with the money market increasingly narrowing the dollar's yield buffer, a test of last week's US$0.7735 low looked in prospect.
"People are waking up to the fact that bill and bond futures here are beginning to think of an easing again," said one.

He noted the 90-day bank bill future, the weathervane for where the market thinks short term official rates are heading, had added another four basis points today to 94.00 exactly matching the current cash rate of 6.00 percent.

This represented a considerable mellowing in attitude since the start of this month when the same contract had been wallowing at 93.77, implying the market saw not the remotest chance of another official easing.
By 12.15 pm (0215 GMT) the currency had taken the hint and caved to US$0.7757/62 having sunk to US$0.7774/79 at the opening from US$0.7815/20 late Monday and a US$0.7895 peak last Friday.

While bill futures were flirting with the idea of another easing here U.S. markets were busy pricing in an entire tightening cycle from the Federal Reserve and money market rates in both countires were converging in response.

Indeed, the process had already seen spreads on one year deposits turn negative, with the U.S. paying around 6.40 percent against 6.00 percent here. Australian dollar forward rates had moved sharply as a result and the one year now stood at 7/11, meaning you had to pay a premium over the spot for the privilege of buying the A$ a year foreward. The same contract stood at -15 at the start of the month and reached as low as -41 in February.

Bond yields were sharing the same trend and the yield on Australian government two-year paper actually moved below that on Treasuries this morning after standing more than 40 basis points above it a few week ago.
At bottomline this meant investors were no longer paid as much, or in some cases had to pay, to hold Australian dollars instead of U.S. dollars, making the currency less attractive as a result.
And analysts could see no end to the trend given the U.S. was far more advance in its economic cycle than Australia.

Dismal domestic employment data last week had shown how slack the labour market was compared to the U.S. and a run of subdued price indicators pointed to abating inflation pressures here while the Fed was having to take pre-emptive strikes against the old demon.

The well behaved partial price data continued today with manufacturing input prices falling 0.5 percent in February for an annual drop of 3.8 percent. This followed subdued output price data released Monday and reinforced analysts expectations of a further slowdown in consumer price inflation when the March quarter figures are released next week.

With analysts confidently expecting the key underlying rate of inflation to reach the very bottom of the Reserve Bank's 2-3 percent target band, or even fall below it, the scope would appear to be there for another easing in policy should the bank think it warranted.

In the very long term, however, should Australia manage to keep inflation below that in the U.S. it should prove positive for the local dollar since it implied Australian producers were becoming more competitive on price vis-a-vis their U.S. competitors.
